name: Northern Khmer
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Krissana Yodmongkhon 1986, The phonological study of Northern Khmer (Prakhonchai district, Buriram province), 182pp. (per Glottolog nort2684 refs)

new_statements.quote: There are 3 degrees of stress: primary or strong, secondary or moderate, and tertiary or weak. Primary and secondary stress are represented by the acute and grave respectively while tertiary stress is unmarked. As in the standard, monosyllables uttered in isolation take primary stress: /báan/ '[I] can [do it]', /srúuəl/ '[It's] easy'; dissyllables of native provenance take primary stress on the ultima: /cənnə́ər/ 'ladder', /ləmbáak/ 'trouble'. The same pattern obtains in dissyllabic compounds: /koon kóon/ 'children', /pləəw tnɔ́l/ 'road, highway'. Polysyllables take primary stress on the ultima, secondary stress on the first syllable: /tòorəsáp/ 'telephone', /wìtsəwɔkɔ́ɔn/ 'engineer'.
new_statements.citation: Jenner, Philip N. 1974. Observations on the Surin dialect of Khmer. In Nguyen Dang Liem (ed.), South-East Asian Linguistic Studies, Vol. 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-31), 61-74. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-C31.61 (online edition CC BY-SA 4.0).
new_statements.locator: sec. 2 Suprasegmentals, 2.1 Stress, p. 66 (PDF page 74 of PL-C31)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (strong) stress falls on the last syllable of the word: monosyllables are stressed; native disyllables (minor + major syllable) and disyllabic compounds stress the ultima; polysyllables (loans) stress the ultima with secondary stress on the first syllable. Stress is non-contrastive and predictable from position/syllable type: the stressed syllable is the word-final major syllable, minor syllables (presyllables) carry weak or no stress (confirmed independently by Yodmongkhon 1986 p. 80, Prakorb 1987 pp. 113, 213-214, Ponchanok 2016 p. 97/139).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Jenner: secondary (moderate) stress on the first syllable of polysyllables, e.g. /tòorəsáp/ 'telephone'; three degrees (primary/secondary/tertiary). Yodmongkhon 1986 p. 80 and Prakorb 1987 p. 214 likewise distinguish strong stress (major syllable), weak stress (minor syllable of shape CVN / 'type C') and non-stress (open minor syllables / presyllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Jenner restricts the disyllable rule to words 'of native provenance' and treats polysyllables (mostly loans) separately (still ultima). Prakorb 1987 p. 214 and Yodmongkhon 1986 p. 80 state stress is non-contrastive and need not be marked phonemically; Ponchanok 2016 (Sisaket) says the major syllable is 'usually' the last syllable and stress is non-phonemic. Smalley 1976 p. 48: Northern Khmer is not a tonal language; Jenner p. 61: register is absent in Surin.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolation/citation forms (Jenner p. 66 explicitly: 'monosyllables uttered in isolation take primary stress'). Jenner adds a phrase-level rule on the same page: 'Within the phrase qualifying elements take primary stress, qualified elements secondary or tertiary stress', with four clause-terminal intonation contours described in 2.2 (p. 66-67). The Mahidol theses treat stress at the 'phonological word' rank (one strong-stressed major syllable as nucleus, optional preceding weak/unstressed minor syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: Jenner 1974 describes the Surin (town) dialect from one informant (Aree Somthawin); Yodmongkhon 1986 the Prakhonchai (Buriram) dialect; Prakorb 1987 the Surin dialect; Ponchanok 2016 the Takhian Ram (Sisaket) dialect; Smalley 1976 Surin-area speech. All are sub-dialects of nort2684 with no separate Glottolog codes; they agree on the stress facts. Glottolog also files Chanthaburi and Chachoengsao Khmer (Wayland & Jongman 2001; Wichitkhachee 1996) under nort2684, but those are western-Thailand varieties, not the Surin/Buriram/Sisaket bloc described here.

sources.note: p. 78: 'The phonological word of Northern Khmer has one strong stressed syllable as its nucleus, and may have one preceeding syllable which has weak stress or non-stress as its periphery.' p. 79: disyllabic word = minor syllable (periphery) followed by major syllable (nucleus). p. 80 sec. 4.3 Word Stress: 'There are three types of stress in this study: strong stress, weak stress and non-stress. Strong stress... is always on major syllable and occurs in monosyllabic word... Its marker is not needed in phonemic writing. Weak Stress... is always on minor syllable type C... of disyllabic word...…

sources.citation: Smalley, William A. 1976. The problem of vowels: Northern Khmer. In W. A. Smalley (ed.), Phonemes and orthography: language planning in ten minority languages of Thailand (Pacific Linguistics C-43), 43-84. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: p. 48: 'Northern Khmer is not a tonal language'; presyllables are 'very short, unstressed syllables in which the vowel is extremely short and glided over'. Orthography-oriented sketch; no explicit word-stress rule (author says the analysis is 'sketchy and tentative', p. 43-44).
